newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Bruton, Major to discuss Northern Ireland crisis.
newsitem.headline: Bruton, Major to discuss Northern Ireland crisis.

text.p: British and Irish prime ministers John Major and John Bruton will discuss the threat of violence against their cherished two-year Northern Ireland peace process at European Union summit talks on Saturday.
They will take time off from EU business to exchange ideas on how to breathe life into a process under assault from both pro-Irish IRA guerrillas and pro-British Protestant militia.

Their talks take place amid gloom amongst Irish officials about the snail's pace of four-month-old peace talks in Belfast and hostility from the province's key Protestant Unionist parties to Dublin's involvement in the process.

The atmosphere has been further clouded by veiled threats from Protestant militia to end a two-year ceasefire in their murky war against Northern Ireland Roman Catholics in retaliation for IRA (Irish Republican Army) violence.
The IRA, at war against British rule of the province for 27 years, ended a 17-month politically-inspired ceasefire in February with publicity-grabbing attacks in Britain and Germany.

But it has so far refrained from any bombings or shootings in Northern Ireland itself. Police fear that if Protestant "Loyalist" groups abandon the truce, it could provoke reprisals by the IRA and bring conflict back to the province of 1.5 million people.
The IRA's political wing, Sinn Fein, is excluded from the faltering peace talks which have yet to address a single substantive issue since they opened in June.
The Province's Protestant Unionist parties, which want to stay for ever British, suspect Major and Bruton of trying to bend the rules of admission to ensure that Sinn Fein take part.
At issue is "decommissioning", the surrender of guerrilla weapons, the main stumbling block in the peace process since it was launched in December 1994.
Unionists want the two governments to introduce legislation saying that disarmament should be the first issue on the agenda and that it has to be carried out before the talks progress.

Unionists insist on this formula for fear that the two governments will relax the rules to try to get representatives of the IRA, whose war is at the heart of the conflict, to the negotiating table for the first time.
Bruton and Major are expected to issue fresh appeals for a new IRA ceasefire despite indications that the guerrillas are on a new campaign in Britain which could wreck the peace talks.

Sir John Wheeler, Northern Ireland Office security minister, said on Thursday that an IRA arms find in London last week prevented an IRA "spectacular" attack designed to force a crisis in the peace process.
"This material was clearly intended for use in a terrorist "spectacular' on the lines of those at Docklands and Manchester," Wheeler said.
The IRA attacked the London Docklands and the northern city of Manchester this year to try to get Britain and Ireland to drop any preconditions for Sin Fein's entry to the peace talks.
